proof_summary: Writing the term as \(q=((m+7)^2-2)/\gcd((m+7)^2-2,\,2(m+6)(m+4)!)\), factorial divisibility and growth estimates show—after finitely many exceptional cases—that every prime \(p\mid q\) either satisfies \(p\ge m+7\) or already has \(q=p\). If \(q\) were composite and not 1, two prime factors would therefore have product at least \((m+7)^2\), contradicting both their product dividing \(q\) and \(q\mid (m+7)^2-2\).
